title: What is a case interview, and what are interviewers really looking for?
description: What a case interview is, the two formats you will meet, and the six things every interviewer scores.
hook: If you have a case interview coming up and you are not quite sure what will happen in the room, you are not alone. Most people walk into their first case feeling they are supposed to already know the answer. You are not. This guide explains what a case interview actually is, the two formats you will meet, and the six things interviewers quietly score you on, so you can stop guessing and start preparing for the right thing.
body:
In this guide

  • What you are actually being tested on
  • The two formats
  • The six things interviewers score
  • A worked example
  • What to remember
  • Check yourself

What you are actually being tested on

A case interview is usually a 20-40 minute conversation about a business problem: profits are falling, should we enter this market, what should we charge. You are not expected to know the answer. You are expected to think like a consultant in front of the interviewer: break the problem into parts, find the part that matters, use numbers to test your ideas, and finish with a clear recommendation.

Interviewers are really asking two questions. Can this person solve the problem? And would I put this person in front of a client? The second question is judged on every sentence you say, which is why this course spends a whole lesson on how you come across.

The two formats

Interviewer-led cases (common at McKinsey) move question by question. The interviewer asks for a structure, then a calculation, then a chart reading, then a recommendation. Each question is scored on its own.

Candidate-led cases (common at BCG, Bain and most other firms) give you a prompt and expect you to drive. You decide what to look at next and ask for the data you need. Waiting to be told what to do is the most common way to lose these cases.

Prepare for both. The skills are the same; what changes is who holds the steering wheel.

The six things interviewers score

Firms' scorecards differ, but most cover these six things, and the PrepForCase case log scores you on exactly these:

  • Clarify and recap: did you understand the problem and the goal?
  • Structure and hypothesis: did you break it down sensibly and say where you'd start?
  • Maths and charts: were your numbers right, and did you draw the insight?
  • Case leadership: did you drive the case forward?
  • Recommendation: did you give a clear answer with reasons?
  • Communication: were you clear, calm and easy to follow?

See it in action: What a case sounds like in the first two minutes

Interviewer: "Our client is a regional bakery chain. Sales are flat but profits have fallen by a third. The CEO wants to know why."

Strong candidate: "So a regional bakery chain, flat sales, profit down a third, and we need to find out why and presumably fix it. Before I structure, two quick questions: is the goal to get back to the previous profit level, and by when? And is the whole bakery industry seeing this, or just our client?"

Notice what happened: a short recap, a check on the goal, and one question that splits the whole problem in two (industry-wide or company-specific).

What to remember

  • Nobody expects you to know the answer; they want to watch you think.
  • You are judged on solving the case and on how you come across while you do it.
  • Six stages get scored. Practise all six, not just structuring.

Check yourself

Have a go at each one before you open the answer. Getting some wrong is how it sticks.

1. In a candidate-led case, what is the most common way to lose points?

  • Asking too many clarifying questions
  • Waiting for the interviewer to say what to do next
  • Using a framework you learnt from a book
Show the answer

Waiting for the interviewer to say what to do next. Candidate-led cases reward you for driving. After every answer, say where you want to go next and why.

2. Which question best splits a profitability case in two?

  • How many employees does the client have?
  • Is the whole industry affected, or just our client?
  • Who is the CEO?
Show the answer

Is the whole industry affected, or just our client?. Industry-wide problems point to market causes; company-only problems point to the client’s own revenue or costs.

Try it now

Your interviewer says: "Our client, a cinema chain, has seen ticket sales fall 15% in two years. What’s going on?" Write the ONE clarifying question that would split this problem in two.

Give yourself 60 seconds, out loud if you can. Speaking it, rather than thinking it, is what builds the skill.

Show a strong answer

"Is the whole cinema industry seeing this decline, or just our client?" If it’s industry-wide, look at streaming, release schedules and habits. If it’s only our client, look at our locations, prices, film choice and experience.
outro: You do not have to get all of this right at once. Pick one thing from this guide to focus on in your next practice case. This guide is lesson 1 of the free PrepForCase course, where you can do the exercise and quiz and track your progress.
